evidence.note: Ad hoc but reasonably systematic curl checks of HTTP main paths and error codes: register, login, workspace, channel, empty-message validation, invalid username — confirms basic status-code behavior.
Cross-node testing: read workspace from node 1, post via node 2, and explicitly verified dense per-channel seq {1,2,3} across nodes — a real invariant check, but only for HTTP writers.
Actively killed HTTP node 2 and verified nodes 0/1 still serve reads/writes, then restarted node 2 and confirmed catch-up via shared SQLite — genuine node-kill resilience testing (part of anchor 8).
IRC exercised only at the auth/shrug level (464 bad auth, 001-005 welcome, /shrug Unicode); no join/names/privmsg bridging or mixed HTTP+IRC seq-density verification.

WebSocket never truly exercised — only 'endpoint accessibility'/port checks; broadcast-kill scenario never simulated (just confirmed ports 9000-9002 listening); resume.gap and exactly-once fan-out untested.
SPA verified only by counting data-testids in served HTML (65/66 then fixed); never driven by an automated browser against the pinned selectors.

reasoning: The agent exercised each subsystem's main HTTP paths and error codes, checked cross-node dense seq, and — going beyond anchor 5 — actively killed an HTTP node and verified continued reads/writes plus restart catch-up. But it never tested the broadcast-kill scenario, never did a real WebSocket subscribe/resume/seq test, never verified mixed HTTP+IRC seq density or resume.gap, and never drove the SPA in a browser. This lands between anchor 5 (main paths + thin resilience) and anchor 8 (all four transports with invariant checks plus both kill scenarios), closer to 5 but elevated by the genuine HTTP-node-kill + cross-node seq verification — a 6.
